one_liner: Per-thread counters spaced 128 bytes apart instead of in adjacent array slots, removing false sharing; book demo, not a library.
what_it_does: Chapter05/04_local_incr.C gives every Google Benchmark thread its own unsigned long counter, increments it 1024 times per iteration, then adds it into one shared std::atomic. BM_false_shared takes the counter from x2a[thread_index], so up to eight threads' counters sit in one 64-byte line; BM_not_shared takes x3a[16*thread_index], a 128-byte stride, so each counter has a line to itself. The lesson is a layout rule, not an API: data written by different threads should not share a cache line.
how_it_is_fast: Caches stay coherent per cache line, so when threads write different words of the same line the line moves between their caches on every write and each store waits for ownership even though no data is logically shared (false sharing). Spacing the counters 16 unsigned longs apart puts each on its own line, so increments stay in the writing core's cache and threads run independently. The 128-byte stride also separates adjacent-line pairs: folly sets its hardware_destructive_interference_size to 128 on non-ARM targets because its microbenchmarks saw destructive interference between line pairs under heavy atomic increments on Sandy Bridge.
when_to_use: Per-thread counters, partial sums, histograms or statistics slots kept in an array indexed by thread id and written in a hot loop.
Thread pools or split loops where each worker writes its own result slot or progress field next to other workers' slots.
Hot fields that ended up adjacent by accident (consecutive globals, an array of small per-thread structs): pad them or give them alignas(64) or a 128-byte stride.
Scaling a counter past one shared atomic: accumulate per thread on separate lines and fold into the shared total rarely, as this harness does once per 1024 increments.
when_not_to_use: Single-threaded code or data that threads only read: there is no false sharing to remove, and the book's own claim is that the effect is absent at one thread.
Large per-element arrays: padding 8-byte values to 64 or 128 bytes multiplies memory and cache footprint 8 to 16 times, which can cost more than it saves.
Data that threads genuinely share (one counter everyone updates): padding does nothing for true sharing; use per-thread copies or a different algorithm.
Expecting a fixed speedup: the 'about twice as fast' figure is one book chart on an unstated CPU, and the gain grows with thread count and write rate.

integration.dependencies: none for the technique; the benchmark file needs Google Benchmark and POSIX headers (unistd.h for sysconf)
integration.min_toolchain: any C++ for manual stride padding, C++11 for alignas(64), C++17 for std::hardware_destructive_interference_size; the benchmark file needs Google Benchmark 1.5.x or older because it reads state.thread_index as a data member
integration.platforms: any; folly assumes 64-byte destructive interference on ARM and s390x and 128 bytes elsewhere, so a 128-byte stride is the conservative choice
integration.thread_safety: Each padded slot must be written by one thread only; whoever sums the slots needs atomics or a join/barrier to see final values (the harness folds each counter into a std::atomic).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same code with a stride or alignas change, but the array grows 8 to 16 times and indexing changes from x[i] to x[16*i] or to an array of aligned structs

gotchas: x3a is a plain unsigned long array without alignas; the padding comes only from the 16-element (128-byte) stride, which is enough for one 8-byte counter per thread but not for larger per-thread structs, which need alignas(64) or alignas(128) on the struct as 02_sharing_incr.C does with __attribute__((aligned(64))).

02_sharing_incr.C uses GCC's __attribute__((aligned(64))) and every file uses unistd.h and sysconf, so the code builds with GCC or Clang on POSIX only, although the README lists Visual Studio and Windows; use standard alignas when copying.

std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is not a safe ABI constant: GCC warns (-Winterference-size) that its value can vary between compiler versions or -mtune/-mcpu flags, and folly suppresses that warning only on the assumption that the whole application is built with the same options; use a fixed 64 or 128 in public headers.

The file reads state.thread_index as a data member, which Google Benchmark v1.6.0 (PR #1208, merged 2021-08-23) made private behind thread_index(), so it must be edited to compile against current releases; there is no Makefile or CMake file. The sweep runs 1 to sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_CONF) unpinned threads including SMT siblings, and the shared accumulators x2 and x3 are unpadded globals next to the arrays, so their placement relative to thread 0's counter is up to the compiler and linker.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The sibling 'alignas(64) per-thread result slots' entry from Asynchronous Programming with C++ shows the same fix with a much larger book figure (4403 ms against 160 ms, about 27x) and the cleaner alignas(64) form; this entry adds a Google Benchmark sweep over thread counts and a 128-byte stride that also covers adjacent-line pairs. Against the atomic-counter siblings, per-thread padded counters folded into one atomic are the usual next step when a single shared atomic becomes the bottleneck.
verified_claims_summary: The book, relayed by the seed lead, reports that with the counters on separate cache lines the per-thread accumulation stays about twice as fast as with adjacent counters (Figure 5.8) and keeps scaling with thread count; the ratio is the author's own, read from a chart, with no CPU model, compiler, flags or results file in the repository. The checked-in harness is symmetric (the same 1024 increments and one shared atomic add per iteration in both variants), so the comparison is fair, but the figure cannot be reproduced from the repository alone.
status_note: MIT-licensed Packt companion repository (405 stars, 91 forks, not archived); Chapter05 has not changed since the September 2021 folder rename and the last commit is 2024-05-13, so copy the layout rule (alignas(64) or a 128-byte stride) rather than the harness.
